{{short description|Technique used to compare populations with different age profiles}}
In [[epidemiology]] and [[demography]], '''age adjustment''', also called '''age standardization''', is a technique used to allow [[statistical population]]s to be compared when the age profiles of the populations are quite different.

==Example==
For example, in 2004/5, two Australian health surveys investigated rates of long-term [[circulatory system]] health problems (e.g. [[heart disease]]) in the general Australian population, and specifically in the [[Indigenous Australian]] population. In each age category over age 24, Indigenous Australians had markedly higher rates of circulatory disease than the general population: 5% vs 2% in age group 25–34, 12% vs 4% in age group 35–44, 22% vs 14% in age group 45–54, and 42% vs 33% in age group 55+.<ref name="NATSIHS">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ausstats.abs.gov.au/ausstats/subscriber.nsf/0/B1BCF4E6DD320A0BCA25714C001822BC/$File/47150_2004-05.pdf|title=National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey|access-date=2009-01-12|publisher=Australian Bureau of Statistics|year=2006}}</ref>

However, overall, these surveys estimated that 12% of all Indigenous Australians had long-term circulatory problems<ref name="NATSIHS"/> compared to 18% of the overall Australian population.<ref name="NHS">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ausstats.abs.gov.au/ausstats/subscriber.nsf/0/3B1917236618A042CA25711F00185526/$File/43640_2004-05.pdf|title=National Health Survey: Summary of results|access-date=2009-01-12|publisher=Australian Bureau of Statistics|year=2006}}</ref>

==Standard populations==

In order to adjust for age, a standard population must be selected. Some agencies which produce health statistics also publish standard populations for age adjustment.  Standard populations have been developed for specific countries<ref name="US">{{cite web |url=https://aspe.hhs.gov/collaborations-committees-advisory-groups/hhs-data/hhs-data-council-introduction/dc-archive/hhs-policy-changing-population-standard-age-adjusting-death-rates-82698 |title=Policy statement on changing the population standard used for age adjusting death rates in DHHS publications |last1=Shalala |first1=D.E. |date=August 26, 1998 |access-date=May 24, 2014}}</ref> and regions.<ref name="euro">{{cite tech report |first=M. |last=Pace |author2=G. Lanzieri |author3=M. Glickman|author4=E. Grande |author5=T .Zupanic | author6=B. Wojtyniak |author7=M. Gissler |author8=E. Cayotte |author9=L. Agafitei | display-authors = 8|title=Revision of the European Standard Population  |series=Methodologies and Working papers |institution= Eurostat|year= 2013|url=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/5926869/KS-RA-13-028-EN.PDF}}</ref>  World standard populations have also been developed to compare data from different countries, including the Segi World Standard and the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) standard.<ref name="WHO">{{cite tech report |first=O.B. |last=Ahmad |author2=C. Boschi-Pinto |author3=A.D. Lopez|author4= C.J.L. Murray|author5=R. Lozano| author6=M. Inoue|title= AGE STANDARDIZATION OF RATES: A NEW WHO STANDARD|series= GPE Discussion Paper Series: No.31|institution= World Health Organization (WHO)|year= 2001|url=https://www.who.int/healthinfo/paper31.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20220401221352/https://www.who.int/healthinfo/paper31.pdf|archive-date=2022-04-01}}</ref> These agencies must balance between setting weights which may be used over a long period of time, which maximizes comparability of published statistics, and revising weights to be close to the current age distribution. When comparing data from a specific country or region, using a standard population from that country or region means that the age-adjusted rates are similar to the true population rates.<ref name="SBODrates">{{cite journal |vauthors=Wyper GM, Grant I, Fletcher E, McCartney G, Fischbacher C, Stockton DL | title=How do world and European standard populations impact burden of disease studies? A case study of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in Scotland | journal=Archives of Public Health | year= 2020 | volume= 78 | issue= 1 | article-number=1 | pmid=31908777 | doi=10.1186/s13690-019-0383-8 | pmc=6941317 | doi-access=free }}</ref>  On the other hand, standardizing data using a widely used standard such as the WHO standard population allows for easier comparison with published statistics.
